question: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) can be diagnosed at post-mortem when histopathology shows no definitive cause of death, and is therefore a diagnosis that automatically excludes homicide.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. SIDS is a diagnosis of exclusion, not an automatic finding when no cause is found. Smothering can produce a completely negative autopsy identical to SIDS. The forensic pathologist must integrate post-mortem findings with scene investigation and history before reaching SIDS as a conclusion. It does not exclude homicide without this full investigation.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. SIDS is a diagnosis of exclusion — it requires a thorough post-mortem examination, scene investigation, and clinical history review, with no identifiable cause of death found. Importantly, a diagnosis of SIDS does not automatically exclude homicide. Smothering (suffocation) may leave no histopathological findings and can mimic SIDS. A full investigation including scene examination and maternal/family assessment is required before SIDS is concluded.
